task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-05-23, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: defining PNR failure from play-by-play derived possessions
identifying counter actions (pull-up) following failed PNR
unit of analysis for league-wide proportion and median lift
sample size and power for per-unit lift estimation
null hypothesis testing for lift > 0 in ≥70% of units and median lift > 2pp
confounding by game situation, score, opponent quality
regression to the mean after selecting on negative PNR outcome
operationalization of lift metric (points per possession)
multiple testing across units and thresholds
evidence_establishes: No prior study-family records were returned; no earlier findings are available from this project.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the counter effect exists at the league-wide scale.
Whether the proposed lift thresholds are realistic or tested before.
Which operational definitions of PNR failure and pull-up counter produce reliable signals.
own_inferences: The question is testing a specific claim about a league-wide counter strategy: after a defensive stop on a PNR, offenses that utilize pull-up shots should show a systematic efficiency gain across most contexts.
The data can plausibly support such a test, provided clear definitions are made and a within-unit comparison mitigates confounders.
The greatest threat is low per-unit sample size, which could make the threshold tests (70% of units, median 2pp) underpowered even if an effect exists.

Using the difference in pull-up efficiency after failed vs. successful PNR as the lift metric helps control for game situation and team quality, but some residual confounding and regression-to-the-mean effects may remain.
uncertainties: Optimal definition of PNR failure (turnover, missed shot, low PPP) impacts sample size and construct validity.
Temporal linkage: should counter be measured on the immediate next possession, within a window, or by a shift in play-type mix over subsequent possessions?
Whether 2pp lift (0.02 points per possession) is a meaningful effect size for team-level payoffs and detectable with available possessions.
Exact unit of analysis (team-season, team-opponent-season, player-pair) not specified; choice influences power and independence.
Stability of the counter relationship across the four available seasons (stationarity) and across regular season vs. playoffs.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical evidence was retrieved, so the decision is based solely on assessment of the research question against the data and methodological principles, without influence from earlier work.

blocking_constraints.text: Per-unit sequences of failed PNR followed by pull-up may be too sparse to accurately estimate lift, threatening the ability to test the 70% proportion and 2pp median thresholds across units.
If units are defined at a granular level (e.g., team-opponent), many will have zero or very few qualifying sequences, making unit-level lift estimates undefined or highly unstable.
Game situation (score, time, quarter, opponent strength) jointly influences PNR outcome, counter play selection, and pull-up efficiency, potentially biasing lift estimates if not controlled.

Conditioning on a negative PNR outcome can induce regression-to-the-mean in subsequent offensive performance; comparing against an appropriate baseline (e.g., after successful PNR) is necessary but may not fully eliminate the bias.

The operational definition of PNR failure and identification of pull‑up counters depend on the accuracy of the derived play-type possession records; misclassification could attenuate or inflate the estimated lift signal.

prior_work.summary: No earlier project studies were found, so it is unknown whether similar questions have been addressed elsewhere.

risks.text: Power to reject the null that lift ≤ 0 in each unit, and to test the 70% threshold, depends on number of qualifying sequences per unit; even across four seasons, some units may have < 50 counter observations.
Units with zero counter exposures can bias proportion estimates if appropriately handled, but handling adds complexity.
Even with a within-unit differencing design, dynamic factors like defensive pressure, lineup changes, and shot clock context may confound the lift measurement.

After a failed PNR, overall offensive efficiency may regress positively; the proposed comparison (after failed vs after successful PNR) reduces but does not eliminate this risk if PNR outcome is correlated with subsequent pull-up quality.
Binary failure classification of PNR possessions relies on accurate shot result and turnover data; mis-tagged plays could create spurious lift signals.
Testing both the proportion ≥ 70% and the median > 2pp introduces a small multiplicity concern, but can be addressed with a joint decision rule.
Play-style evolution across four seasons could make the counter effect non-stationary; pooling seasons assumes stability that may not hold.

design.estimand: Unit-level lift = (PPP of pull-up possessions immediately following a failed PNR possession) minus (PPP of pull-up possessions immediately following a successful PNR possession). A failure is a PNR possession with zero points (turnover or defensive rebound), a success is a PNR possession with ≥ 2 points. Both are counted only when the next offensive possession by the same team is a pull-up play type.
design.unit: Team-season (30 teams × 4 regular seasons = 120 units). Secondary sensitivity analysis with team-opponent-season units, including only matchups with ≥ 30 counter sequences.
design.sample: All regular-season possessions from 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26 in which a PNR possession is immediately followed by a pull-up possession by the same team, excluding possessions with a substitution timeout or end of quarter in between. Playoff data excluded for primary analysis to avoid structural differences.
design.power: Power analysis based on historical variance of pull-up PPP: assuming 80 counter opportunities per unit-season (approx 20 opportunistic PPP samples each in failure and success groups) and per-possession SD 0.4, SE of lift ≈ 0.04 pp. A true lift of 0.02 pp would not be significant per unit. The binomial test for proportion positive will have 80% power to detect a true proportion of 0.7 against a null of 0.5 with n=120 units. The sign test for median > 0.02 requires a high true median (>0.03) to achieve 80% power; with n=120, detectable median ≈ 0.02 pp if 70% of true lifts exceed 0.02. Detailed power simulation recommended before analysis.
design.controls: The differencing design (failure minus success) controls for game situation, team offensive quality, and opponent defensive quality because both conditions occur within the same unit under similar context. Additional robustness checks will control for score margin, period, and remaining shot clock using stratified or regression adjustment.
design.falsification: Compute the same lift metric for an implausible counter (e.g., post-up plays after failed PNR) where no counter relationship is expected. A significant effect there would indicate confounding or design artifacts. Also, check that PNR success/failure distinction is not capturing a difference in pull-up difficulty (e.g., via shot distance, defender distance) using matchup data.
design.multiplicity: Joint test: the null hypothesis is that either the proportion of units with positive lift is ≤ 0.70 OR the median lift across units is ≤ 0.02 pp. Rejection requires both a one-sided exact binomial test p < 0.05 for the proportion > 0.70 and a one-sided sign test p < 0.05 for median > 0.02. No further multiplicity adjustment needed.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null and conclude the counter is real if both p-values < 0.05. Otherwise, fail to reject. Pre-register thresholds and operational definitions, including specification of minimum number of sequences per unit (e.g., ≥ 20) required for inclusion.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files processed for play-by-play and derived play-type possessions covering 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons, as per the data catalog snapshot of 2026-05-23.
